text: Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute. Gilead was his father.
Gilead's wife also bore him sons, and when her sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out. "You will inherit nothing in our father's house," they told him, "for you are the son of another woman."
So Jephthah fled from his brothers and settled in the land of Tob. There worthless men gathered around him and went out with him.
Some time later the Ammonites made war against Israel.
When the Ammonites attacked Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah back from the land of Tob.
"Come," they said to him, "be our commander, so we can fight the Ammonites."
But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Weren't you the ones who hated me and drove me out of my father's house? Why do you come to me now, when you are in trouble?"
The elders of Gilead answered, "That is why we have turned to you now. Come with us and fight the Ammonites, and you shall be head over all of us who live in Gilead."
Jephthah said to them, "If you bring me back to fight the Ammonites, and the LORD gives them over to me, then I will be your head."
The elders of Gilead replied, "The LORD is our witness: we will surely do as you say."
So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him their head and commander. And Jephthah repeated all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.
Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites, asking, "What do you have against me, that you have come to make war in my land?"
The king of the Ammonites answered Jephthah's messengers, "When Israel came up out of Egypt, they took my land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan. Now give those lands back peaceably."

versions.text: The king of the Ammonites answered Jephthah's messengers, "When Israel came up out of Egypt, they took my land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan. Now give it back peaceably."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew object is plural (אֶתְהֶן, "them"), referring to the territories just listed. The singular "it" loses this and reads ambiguously when spoken aloud.

text: Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites once again,
saying to him: "This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites.
When they came up from Egypt, Israel traveled through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh.

Then Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, 'Please let us pass through your land.' But the king of Edom would not listen. They also sent to the king of Moab, and he refused. So Israel stayed at Kadesh.

Then they journeyed through the wilderness, went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab, and came to the east side of the land of Moab, where they camped on the far side of the Arnon. They did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was Moab's border.
Israel then sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon, and said to him, 'Please let us pass through your land to our own place.'
But Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory. He mustered all his troops, camped at Jahaz, and fought against Israel.
And the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his troops into Israel's hand, and they struck them down. So Israel took possession of the whole land of the Amorites who lived in that country.
They took possession of all Amorite territory, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
Now then, the LORD, the God of Israel, drove out the Amorites before his people Israel—and you would take possession of it?
Will you not take possession of whatever Chemosh your god gives you? So we will take possession of whatever the LORD our God has driven out before us.

versions.text: Do you not hold what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? So we will possess whatever the LORD our God has given us.
versions.explanation: "Do you not hold" is awkward and blurs the verb יָרַשׁ ("take possession of"). The second half also drops the sense of הוֹרִישׁ מִפָּנֵינוּ ("dispossessed before us"), which is the parallel that carries the argument.

text: Are you any better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever quarrel with Israel or go to war against them?
For three hundred years Israel has lived in Heshbon and its villages, in Aroer and its villages, and in all the towns along the Arnon. Why did you not reclaim them in all that time?
I have not wronged you, but you are doing me wrong by making war on me. Let the LORD, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites."
But the king of the Ammonites paid no attention to the message Jephthah sent him.
Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah. He crossed through Gilead and Manasseh, passed by Mizpah of Gilead, and from there advanced against the Ammonites.
And Jephthah made a vow to the LORD: "If you give the Ammonites into my hand,
then whoever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return safely from the Ammonites shall belong to the LORD, and I will offer him up as a burnt offering.

versions.text: then whoever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return in triumph from the Ammonites shall belong to the LORD, and I will offer him up as a burnt offering."
versions.explanation: בְשָׁלוֹם means "in peace/safely," not "in triumph." The interpretive rendering adds a note of victory the Hebrew does not state here.

text: So Jephthah crossed over to fight the Ammonites, and the LORD gave them into his hand.
He struck them down from Aroer to the outskirts of Minnith—twenty towns—and as far as Abel Keramim. It was a crushing blow, and the Ammonites were subdued before the Israelites.

versions.text: He devastated twenty towns from Aroer to the vicinity of Minnith, as far as Abel Keramim. It was a crushing defeat, and the Ammonites were subdued before the Israelites.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb וַיַּכֵּם has a pronoun object ("he struck them," i.e. the Ammonites); the current wording makes the towns the object and drops the reference to the people who were defeated.

text: When Jephthah came home to Mizpah, there was his daughter, coming out to meet him with tambourines and dancing. She was his only child; he had no other son or daughter.
When he saw her, he tore his clothes and cried, "Oh, my daughter! You have brought me to my knees; you have become the cause of my ruin. I have opened my mouth to the LORD and I cannot take it back."
She said to him, "My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD. Do to me as you have vowed, now that the LORD has avenged you on your enemies, the Ammonites.
She said to her father, "Grant me this one request: give me two months to go and wander the hills with my friends and weep, because I will never marry."

versions.text: But grant me this one request," she said. "Give me two months to roam the hills and weep with my friends, because I will never marry."
versions.explanation: Two small issues: the quotation marks are inconsistent (the speech beginning "But grant me..." is closed but never opened), and the Hebrew has her companions accompanying her ("I and my friends") rather than weeping with her. Recasting with the speech introduction first ("she said to her father") also matches the Hebrew word order and reads more smoothly aloud.

text: "Go," he said, and he let her go for two months. She and her friends went into the hills and wept because she would never marry.
After the two months she returned to her father, and he did to her as he had vowed. She had never known a man. And so it became a custom in Israel

versions.text: After the two months she returned to her father, and he did to her as he had vowed. She never knew a man. And so it became a custom in Israel
versions.explanation: The Hebrew clause is circumstantial and is best rendered as a pluperfect: she had never known a man (i.e., she was still a virgin). "She never knew a man" placed after the report of the vow reads awkwardly in sequence.

text:
that year after year the young women of Israel go out for four days to commemorate the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite.[^1]

[^1]: Or "to lament for"; the Hebrew verb is rare and may mean either to recount or to mourn.

versions.text: that year after year the young women of Israel go out for four days to commemorate the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite.
versions.explanation: The rare Hebrew verb can mean either "recount/commemorate" or "lament," and a brief footnote would help the reader without changing the flow of the reading text.
